D. Threat rows beyond section 10.4

Why

Where to start in the long table. The notes in sections 4 to 9 kept pointing here; this is why. TH8 to TH11 are the rows whose controls the body already built without naming them: the service token (6.1, 10.5) answers TH8, the DuckDB confinement (6.3) answers TH9, the receipt-digest cache key (6.3, 8) answers TH10, the insert-only chained audit (6.3, 10.6) answers TH11. Read those four first and you will recognise each mechanism; TH12 to TH15 (a stolen cookie, injected instructions, denial of service, an out-of-grammar proposal) are the ones a seat, a file or a sentence is enough to attempt, held inside one organization by the epoch, the five tools, the slots and whole-output validation.

The 22 rows 10.4 does not keep, TH8 to TH29, with 10.4's columns and on its scale: the threat in full (actor, prerequisite, action, impact, asset), the invariant at stake, the existing control apart from the new mitigations, the response, and likelihood, impact, status and residual together; every mitigation is [proposed] and the head owns each residual. TH8 to TH11 are High on impact, their controls fixed by 6.3, 8 and 10.5; TH9, TH12 to TH15 and TH20 are High on likelihood; TH19, TH22 and TH29 High on impact; the rest Medium or Low on both.

Why

Why a cache is a threat row. A cache keyed without the organization or the policy epoch serves one scope's answer to another, or a pre-revocation answer after it. The receipt digest as the key carries both, and the hit is still re-authorized before release. Caching is an authorization decision, not a performance one.

Why

The revocation race, as locks. A command holds the membership row FOR SHARE; a revocation takes it FOR UPDATE. The two cannot overlap, so either the command commits under the old epoch before the revocation (and stays in authorized history, with visibility re-checked at delivery) or the revocation lands first and the command sees a stale epoch and is refused. This is the membership epoch (SI4) made concrete, and S06's two-way ordering test proves both orders.

Course

8 lessons that walk the record in its own order. Each names its sections, what you should be able to do afterwards, and how long a careful first read takes. Tick a lesson when you can do what it lists; the tick is kept in this browser.

Lesson 1: What a design document is for

45 minutes · sections 1. Summary, 2. Context and problem statement
  • Explain who reads a design document and what each reader is looking for.
  • Find the sentence that says what the design optimises for, and what it gives up.
  • Retell the problem as a mechanism: the component, the step and the number that fails.
  • Name the one-way doors and say why each is expensive to reverse.

Read the summary twice: once before the rest of the document and once after. The second time you will see how much of it is a promise the body keeps. Then read the context as if you had to solve the problem yourself tomorrow with a different design.

2 design notes in these sections · exercises: 1, 2

Lesson 2: Pinning the target

60 minutes · sections 3. Goals, non-goals, and assumptions, 4. Requirements
  • Tell a goal from a non-goal from an assumption, and say what each one is for.
  • Follow one quality requirement back to the arithmetic that produced its number.
  • Read a latency target written as percentiles and say what it allows.
  • Say which requirements the design deliberately lowers, and why that is honest rather than weak.

Pick one N requirement and rebuild its number on paper from the assumptions in section 3 and the load parameters in 4.2. A factor that appears from nowhere, a peak multiplier say, is a gap the document should have derived; note it. If you can rebuild the number, you now understand the scale the whole design is built for.

6 design notes in these sections · exercises: 3, 4

Lesson 3: The shape

60 minutes · sections 5. Architecture overview
  • Read a system context picture and a container picture, and say what each box and arrow means.
  • Tell the worked scenario back in your own words, end to end.
  • Use the key-decisions table as a map: for any box, find the decision that put it there.
  • Explain the fit check: which number lands on which component.

Cover the text and describe the system from the overview's pictures alone. Then read the scenario and check yourself. The things you got wrong are what the pictures do not say; a good document says them in the narration.

4 design notes in these sections · exercises: 5, 6

Lesson 4: Inside the boxes

75 minutes · sections 6. Component design
  • Read a component card and state the component's one job and what it refuses to do.
  • Find the ceiling of each component and the reason behind it.
  • Read a dependency table and say what happens when each dependency is down.
  • Explain an extension point in the form "to add Y you add Z without editing W".

For each card (a container without a hard choice gets a one-paragraph card with no headings), write the ceiling line in your own words before reading it. Then look at the worked example and change one value: does the mechanism still work? If the answer is not obvious, you have found a corner case the card should have covered.

8 design notes in these sections · exercises: 7, 8, 9, 10

Lesson 5: Following the data

75 minutes · sections 7. Data flows, 8. Data model and storage, 9. API surface
  • Read a data-flow diagram: processes, stores, external entities, and the trust boundaries between them.
  • Follow one flow through its phases to the terminal line, then through its failure cases.
  • Say for each store whether it is the system of record or derived, and what that decides.
  • Read an API sketch and say what a caller sees on permission failure, on a missing object, and on a repeated request.

Take the sequence diagram and, at each step, ask what would happen if the message were forged or lost. The flows are where the threat model comes from, so every answer you write here is a row you will recognise in section 10.

6 design notes in these sections · exercises: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15

Lesson 6: Attacking the design

90 minutes · sections 10. Security and threat model
  • List the invariants and name the component that enforces each.
  • Read a STRIDE row and identify the actor, the prerequisite, the action, the impact and the asset.
  • Tell a preventative mitigation from a detective one, and say why High rows need both.
  • Explain the break-glass path and why operator access is a design question, not a policy.

Start with the trust levels and the assets, not the table. Then pick three rows with High impact, the ones the invariants exist for, and trace each to its data-flow element, its invariant and its security requirement in section 4. If a row does not trace, that is a finding.

8 design notes in these sections · exercises: 16, 17, 18, 19

Lesson 7: Running it

60 minutes · sections 11. Operations
  • Explain the rollout, staged or not, and name what triggers rollback.
  • Read an objective and the indicator that measures it, and say whether an alert measures it; an objective with neither an alert nor a stated reason for none is a finding.
  • Use the failure-modes table: for a given failure, say how it is detected, what mitigates it and what an operator types.
  • Say what changes at ten times the load, and which cost line grows first.

Imagine you are on call tonight. Which dashboard do you open, which alert, if any, would wake you, and what would you do when it did? The section should answer all three without you guessing.

5 design notes in these sections · exercises: 20, 21, 22

Lesson 8: Being honest

60 minutes · sections 12. Alternatives considered, 13. Risks, open questions, objections, and future work, Appendix
  • Read a decision record: drivers, options, the choice, the consequences, the confirmation.
  • Say what each rejected alternative optimises for and why that is wrong here.
  • Rank a risk on the same scale as the threat table and say what failure would look like.
  • Read the objections section and check whether your own first question is there.

Write down the three questions you would ask the author before reading section 13.3. If they are there, the document works; if they are not, you have found either a gap or a question only you would ask, and both are worth knowing.

6 design notes in these sections · exercises: 23, 24, 25

Glossary

231 terms. In the document the first use of each term in every section is a green link; hover to read the definition.

`createResource` (HTML runtime)
a framework data-loading primitive and the framework's module for mounting markup; importing either pulls more framework code into the route, which the 426 B of headroom cannot take (6.5)
`Deprecation` (`Sunset`)
headers announcing that an endpoint will go and when (9)
`FOR UPDATE` (`FOR SHARE`)
row locks: an exclusive one for a row about to change, a shared one that blocks any exclusive lock until the transaction ends (6.3)
`kid`
the key identifier in a token's header that says which key of the key set signed it (6.1)
`Retry-After`
the response header saying when to try again; the only thing the browser retries on (9)
`state`
a random value bound to a short-lived cookie that ties a sign-in callback to the browser that started it (6.1)
`sub` (`tenant_id`)
the token claims naming the person and the organization; the session is minted from these two and nothing else (D6)
0 FAIL gate
the framework's own release check with no failing item (2)
Admission
the control plane's whole-output check of a proposed app definition against the grammar, the registered kinds and operators, the schemas and the complexity limits; it fails whole or produces an admitted digest (C04, 6.2). from the record's glossary
adopt (adopts)
the framework's word for the browser attaching its island code to HTML the server already rendered, what other frameworks call hydration; not adoption of saved work, which appendix A defines (5.2, 6.5)
Adoption
moving saved work from the publication it is pinned to onto a newer one, explicitly, by compare-and-set, after seeing the changes (D14, R10). from the record's glossary
adoption table
rows the publisher writes at publication, one per earlier publication of the app whose record schema the new one can still read, so adoption is a lookup (6.2, 7.3)
advisory lock
a PostgreSQL lock on a number the application chooses, used here so two writers never race on a chain's head (6.3)
ALB (load balancer)
the layer that terminates TLS and spreads requests across tasks (6.6)
anchor
a chain head written to a store nothing can change, so the chain up to that point cannot be rewritten (10.6)
App definition
(AppDefinition): the typed, closed-vocabulary description of an app, proposed by the model as data and rendered by first-party compiled components (C04, D1). from the record's glossary
attack tree
a goal broken into the ways of reaching it, OR by default, AND where all steps are needed (10.4)
authorization code (back channel)
the one-time code the browser carries back from sign-in, exchanged for the token by the server directly, never by browser script (7.2)
availability zone (zone)
one of a region's independent data centres; the design runs in two (11.1)
B-tree (partial index, local)
the ordinary database index, one that covers only rows matching a condition (queued jobs), and "local": one index per unpartitioned table rather than one per partition (8)
bake (baked)
the time a wave runs under watch before the next wave starts (11.1)
blameless postmortem (postmortem)
an incident write-up that names causes and actions, not people (11.4)
blast radius
what a compromise of one boundary can reach, and what it cannot (10.2)
Breakglass
the sealed operator role behind a hardware key whose use alerts a named outside reviewer first (M14, 10.5). from the record's glossary
bridge (way back)
in a migration step, what lets old and new run together, and what lets you retreat (11.1)
burn (budget burning)
spending an error budget faster than its steady rate; the signal AL1 pages on (11.3)
C01 to C16
the shared platform and demo contracts (SHARED-CONTRACTS.md), agreed before this record so the demo and the platform decide the same things; the record restates whatever it relies on, so a C number is a citation, not required reading (cover)
callee
a program the platform calls, as opposed to one that calls the platform; in this release every programmatic party is one, so no API client exists (4.1, 10.5)
callee first (callee-first)
deploying the service that is called before the service that calls it (11.1)
canary name
the canary organization's alias or host on a request, which the rollout routes whole to the new build so the canary's suite runs against every wave (11.1)
Canary organization
a synthetic second organization whose scripted suite replays every call with Northstar's identifiers on every release and must be denied before data (G5). from the record's glossary
Canvas
the spatial surface on which an app's views are arranged, rendered by one browser island from typed props (D10, 6.5). from the record's glossary
cap, not a split
a record hotter than its row lock allows is throttled (429 past 20 waiting), never divided into several rows (8)
capacity units
the load balancer's usage metric, a blend of connections, bandwidth and rule evaluations, priced by the hour on top of the base rate (11.2)
Case
(saved work): one work id pinned to a publication with its bindings, records, notes and personal view state (C02, D14). from the record's glossary
catalog metadata
titles, descriptions, examples and field names of published apps; what retrieval and the provider see instead of rows (D7)
Cell
a separate pool of stores an organization moves to whole, id unchanged, when its load would starve the shared pool (D3, 11.2). from the record's glossary
CloudFront
the content delivery network that serves hash-named assets near the member (6.6)
CloudTrail (CloudWatch)
the cloud's audit log of API calls, and its metrics and logs service (10.5, 11.3)
cold path (warm)
a query whose revision must first be fetched and decrypted, against one already in the node's cache (5.2)
columnar
stored column by column rather than row by row; cheap for aggregates over a few columns (12.2)
compare-and-set
change a value only if it still equals what you last saw; a stale attempt changes zero rows and returns 412 (D14, 8)
compatibility (backward compatible, forward compatible)
old requests still accepted, new responses still readable by old clients (9)
Composer
the assistant that turns an intent into a proposed definition or patch through a generation job the worker runs, behind the provider interface (D8, D13). from the record's glossary
Control plane
the role that admits definitions and alone writes publications, policy and governance audit (D2, 6.2). from the record's glossary
controller (processor)
under data protection law, the party that decides why data is processed and the party that processes it for them; the organization and Forma (10.1)
count mode
a firewall rule setting that records what the rule would have blocked without blocking it; every new rule runs in it first (11.4)
criticality
the order in which work is shed: record commands and published queries last (11.2)
cross-site
a request a hostile site makes to this one with the member's cookie attached; refused as 403 cross_site (9)
Crypto-shredding
making an organization's objects unreadable by disabling and then deleting its data key, after the 24-hour hold (section 8, TH28). from the record's glossary
CSP (nonce)
the content security policy that lets a page run only scripts carrying the per-response random value (TH25)
data classes
Restricted, Confidential and Internal: labels that decide protection and retention per kind of data (10.6)
Data key
the one KMS key per organization under which its objects, index file and exports are encrypted (D3, DS3). from the record's glossary
data protection impact assessment
the risk assessment the GDPR requires of a data controller before high-risk processing (10.1)
Data service
the role that runs typed queries over Parquet through DuckDB and commits record commands in one transaction, every result behind a receipt (D4, 6.3). from the record's glossary
deny by default
anything not explicitly permitted is refused (10.5)
Design point
ten organizations, 100 seats, 30 concurrent users, 60 query operations/s and 2 commits/s at peak (A1, A2, section 4). from the record's glossary
DFD (data-flow diagram)
the picture of processes, stores, external entities and boundaries that the threat table cites (7, 10.2)
digest (content digest)
a SHA-256 hash that names a definition, revision, receipt or result by its exact bytes (6.2)
drain (deregister)
stopping new requests to a task and letting the in-flight ones finish before it stops (11.1)
drill
a rehearsed failure or restore run on purpose to prove a mitigation (11.4)
DuckDB
an embedded analytical database that reads Parquet directly; run here as a locked-down instance per operation (6.3)
ECS (Fargate)
the container service, and its mode where the cloud runs the hosts (D15)
EdDSA
the signature scheme fAuth signs tokens with; verified with a public key, so the platform needs no secret of fAuth's (SR2)
egress
traffic leaving the network; only workers have it to the provider, and it is a cost line (6.4, 11.2)
embed (embedding)
turning text into a vector so similar texts are near each other; done in process here, with no provider call (6.4)
encryption context
a name attached to a key operation that the key policy can require, so a key is used only for the organization it belongs to (TH1, 10.2)
envelope
a data key wrapped by a master key; the master key unwraps it one call at a time (6.6, 10.6)
ephemeral disk
a task's local disk, wiped when the task stops; the revision cache lives there (10.6)
Epoch
a counter advanced by a change of filter (in the browser), membership or policy (in the organization), so a late result or a revoked session is told from a current one (C10, SI4). from the record's glossary
error budget
the share of a window an objective allows to be missed; 99.5% of a month leaves 3.65 hours (N2, 11.3)
expand and contract (expand)
a schema change made in two releases: add the new shape, then remove the old once nothing uses it (11.1)
Expected version
the record version a command was based on; a mismatch is a conflict with an authorized recovery view, never a silent overwrite (D5, C07). from the record's glossary
fail closed (fails closed)
when a control cannot decide, it refuses rather than serves (SR12, 10.6)
failover
the standby taking over as primary, 60 to 120 seconds here (11.4)
fenced commit (fence)
a write that cannot land after a newer claim or a revocation because a lock or a sequence number stands in its way (6.3, 8)
first paint
the moment the server-rendered page is visible, before any JavaScript runs (6.5)
fit check
placing the requirements' numbers on the components that must carry them (5.2)
fixture
fixed synthetic data with known expected numbers that scenarios, tests and drills run against (2, 5)
FMIR
Forma's compiled module format; this record ships only its own compiled modules (review 4.1). from the record's glossary
fuel
a WebAssembly runtime's budget of instructions, after which the module is stopped (6.4)
golden signals (four golden signals)
latency, traffic, errors and saturation, the four things to measure on any service (11.3)
Goodput
the requests served inside their latency target; what overload control preserves first (11.2). from the record's glossary
gp3 (vCPU, GiB, GB)
a storage class, a unit of compute and the two sizes of a gigabyte: GiB is 1,024 cubed bytes, GB is 1,000 cubed; the cost table uses both (11.2)
grammar (query grammar, syntax tree)
the closed set of typed operations a definition may ask for, compiled to the engine from its parsed form and never from text (6.3)
gzip
the compression the route budget is measured under; 28,100 B gzip is the cap on a route's framework code (2, 6.5)
H0 to H11
the head's earlier decisions on design A; this record names them only where it keeps or drops one (3.2, 13.3)
half-open window (half-open)
an interval that includes its start and excludes its end, written [10:00, 10:10), so adjacent windows never share an event (G3, 7.2)
hardware key
a physical security key; required for breakglass and for operators before the first real organization (10.5)
hash chain (hash-chained)
each audit row carries the hash of the one before it, so a deleted or altered row breaks the chain (SR10)
hot record
one record many people commit to at once; one row lock, about 50 commits a second (8)
HttpOnly
a cookie flag that keeps page scripts from reading the cookie (9)
I-1 to I-4
the gaps the foundation review found in the earlier design; R3, R4, N12 and R4's clarifying question close all four (4.1)
IAM authentication
short-lived database credentials issued to a task role instead of a stored password (10.5)
Idempotency key
the key the island mints for every record command and creating request, scoped to organization, principal, work and command, whose outcome a retry returns (D5, section 9). from the record's glossary
idempotency outcome
the stored result of a command under its key, returned unchanged to any retry (6.3, 9)
identity adapter (adapter)
one small component that talks to the sign-in provider and hands the rest of the platform a verified principal, so the provider can change without the rest noticing (1, D6)
index file
one per-organization file of catalog metadata and examples that retrieval searches, rebuilt within 60 s of a publication (D7)
injected instruction
text inside evidence written to steer the model; reaches the provider only as delimited data (TA5, TH13)
invariant
a property that must hold however the environment misbehaves, with the components that enforce it named (10.2)
Island
a browser component Forma attaches to server-rendered HTML; the canvas is one island (D10). from the record's glossary
isolated environment (isolated account)
a separate cloud account a restore is rehearsed into, so the drill touches no live data (N4)
jitter
a random delay added to a retry so many clients do not retry at the same instant (6.4)
Just-in-time access
an operator session over one organization's data, granted by its administrator for an hour and audited (M14, TL5). from the record's glossary
K1 to K5
the head's kickoff rulings for this task, recorded in the intake; K1 is the ruling for a typed definition over markup, K4 for fAuth behind the adapter (cover, 2)
keyless signing (Sigstore)
signing a release with a short-lived certificate tied to the workflow's identity instead of a stored key (TH6)
kmd
the founder's separate notes product, not part of this platform. from the record's glossary
KMS
the key management service holding one data key per organization and the platform's keys (6.6)
KMS-certified key (certifying KMS key)
a role's hourly in-memory signing key, whose public half the role's long-lived asymmetric key in the key service has signed; callees trust the key-service key and so accept the hourly one (6.1, 10.5)
L2 (L3)
the factory's document sizes: L3 the full record this is, L2 the smaller record the demo has (cover)
LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, Core Web Vitals)
the time until the largest element of a page is drawn; one of the browser-measured page quality metrics (N3)
lease (claim sequence)
a time-limited claim on a job, renewed while work continues, with a counter that fences a late result (6.4)
linearizable
every operation appears to happen at one instant in a single order; promised per record (N5)
Little's law
the number of requests in progress equals the arrival rate times the time each one takes; 60 a second times 0.1 s is 6 in flight (5.2)
load shedding (shed)
refusing low-priority work under overload so that high-priority work keeps its latency (11.2)
lockfile
the file pinning every dependency to an exact version and checksum (SR8)
loopback
a server that answers only its own machine; the prototypes' state (2)
MCP Apps
apps rendered inside an assistant such as Claude; deferred past this release (3.2, C14). from the record's glossary
mechanism
a failure told as the step, the component and the number, rather than as an adjective (2)
Membership epoch
the organization's epoch read on every request and held FOR SHARE inside a record command, so revocation and a stale commit serialize (D5, TH21). from the record's glossary
MIT (Apache-2.0, BSD, MPL-2.0)
the permissive open-source licences dependencies may carry, checked in CI (2)
monotonic (monotonic read)
a reader never sees an older state after a newer one; with read-after-write, what the primary promises and a replica may not (8)
mountMarkup (reconcile)
the 3.0.0 runtime's call for mounting markup and the 2.x call the prototypes' widgets use; the prototypes do not mount on 3.0.0 (2)
mTLS
mutual TLS, where both ends of a connection present certificates; rejected here because nobody runs the certificate authority it needs (10.5)
NAT gateway
the managed path that lets private tasks reach the Internet without being reachable from it (11.2)
native subset (subset)
the part of TypeScript the compiler accepts for server-rendered components; a computed comparison is refused (BUILD-610), and appendix B names the other diagnostics (2)
non-Byzantine
a node that may fail or stop but does not lie; the assumption made for nodes inside the VPC (SA1, 10.1)
OAuth (registered client)
the delegation protocol behind the sign-in handoff; the platform is a client fAuth knows by a row, a public one with no secret (6.1, 10.6)
Object Lock
an object storage setting that makes an object undeletable and unchangeable for a period (TH11)
OIDC (OpenID Connect)
the identity protocol over OAuth; here also how the release workflow authenticates to the cloud without a stored key (TH6)
one-way door (two-way door)
a decision expensive to reverse because stored data is in its shape, against one that can be changed later (5.3)
opaque cookie (`__Host-`)
a session cookie that carries only a random id, with the browser prefix that pins it to one host over HTTPS (6.1)
open-loop load
a load test that sends requests at a fixed rate whatever the system's response time, so a slowing system is not spared (N1)
P01 to P16
the product requirements of the validation plan (VALIDATION.md), the criteria the release is judged on; each R line names the ones it answers and the task map lists them (cover, 4.1)
p50 (median)
the value half of the measurements are below; the typical case (N3)
p75
the 75th percentile, the point at which Core Web Vitals assesses a page (N3)
p99 (99th percentile)
the value 99 of 100 measurements are below; the tail the design is held to (N3)
p99.83
the per-operation percentile that makes six operations together meet p99, since 0.9983 to the sixth power is about 0.99 (N3)
Parquet
a columnar file format: values of one column stored together, so a query reads only the columns it needs (D4, 8)
Parquet revision
an immutable columnar copy of an imported source, named by digest, that receipts pin forever (D4, DS2). from the record's glossary
patch (base revision)
a change expressed against a named earlier revision of the definition; a patch on a revision that is no longer current is refused with 412 (R5, D9)
per-query S3 session (S3 session)
temporary cloud credentials minted for one query whose policy allows only that organization's prefix, so even a wrong path is refused by the store (6.3, TH1)
Pin
the publication a case was started on, kept until adoption (R10). from the record's glossary
PKCE
proof key for code exchange: the client sends a hash before sign-in and the secret after, so a stolen authorization code cannot be exchanged by someone else (SR2)
point-in-time recovery
restoring a database to any moment within the backup window, 5-minute granularity here (11.4)
policy epoch (filter epoch)
the policy counter a receipt pins, and the browser's counter per filter change that late pages are compared against (6.5, 8)
pooled tenancy (pooled, pool)
many organizations' rows in one database and one schema, kept apart by keys and policies (1, D3)
pre-aggregation (aggregates at admission)
computing a result ahead of time when a definition is admitted; the fallback if the cold aggregate is too slow (5.2, D4)
principal
the verified identity a request acts as, with its organization, roles and epoch (6.1)
problem+json (problem details)
the standard JSON shape for an HTTP error, with a type and a stable code (9)
provenance
the record of how and from what an artifact was built (SR8)
provider tokens (model tokens)
the units a model provider bills by, in and out; the cost line N10 meters (11.2)
public PKCE client (public client)
an OAuth client that holds no secret because PKCE proves it started the sign-in; the platform's oauth_clients row at fAuth is one (10.6, 6.1)
Publication
the atomic record, written only by the control plane under versioned policy, binding a definition digest, input contracts, record schemas, renderer versions and principals (D2, C09). from the record's glossary
quarantine
taking a revision out of use when its re-derived numbers no longer match its receipts (11.4)
range-read
fetching only the byte ranges of a file a query needs (7.2)
RDS
the managed PostgreSQL service; Multi-AZ means a synchronous standby in a second zone (6.6)
re-derivation
recomputing a cited result from its receipt to check it still matches (SR7, 11.4)
read committed (READ COMMITTED)
the default isolation level: a statement sees what was committed when it started, so cross-row premises need explicit locks (6.3, 8)
read replica
an asynchronous copy for reads that may lag; added at 10x, never for sessions or epochs (11.2)
read-after-write
a reader sees its own committed write; the primary gives this, a lagging replica does not (8)
readiness probe (liveness probe)
the health check that says a task may receive traffic, and the one that says its process is alive (11.1)
real-user telemetry (real-user timing)
latency measured in members' browsers rather than at the server, so it includes the network (N3, 11.3)
Receipt
the server's record of exactly which sources, revisions, operators, parameters, record snapshot and policy epoch produced a result; its digest keys the result cache (C06, section 8). from the record's glossary
Record command
a declared mutation of an app-owned record carrying an expected version and an idempotency key, committed in one PostgreSQL transaction (D5, R8). from the record's glossary
recovery view
the authorized current state returned with a 409, so the member can redo the edit on top of it (D5)
refresh cookie (refresh-cookie bridge)
fAuth's own cross-site cookie on its origin that could keep a browser signed in; the platform does not use it, so nothing cross-site carries authority (TH3)
replay
presenting a captured code, token or approval a second time; every flow here has a check that makes the second use fail (TH3, TH5)
residual
the risk that remains after the mitigations, rated on the same scale (10.4)
retrieval (retrieved, adapted, generated)
the three labels on a creation: found as is, found and changed, or newly proposed (R4)
rotation
replacing a key or secret on a schedule or on suspicion, with the old one revoked (10.6)
Route 53
the DNS service that fails the edge name over on health checks (11.4)
row group
a horizontal slice of a Parquet file; sorting by time lets a window skip the groups it does not overlap (8)
row lock
a lock on one row; two commands on one record wait for each other on it (5.2, 8)
Row-level security
PostgreSQL policies that filter every table by the session's organization, the second wall behind the session-derived scope (D3, SI1). from the record's glossary
RPO (recovery point objective)
how much recent data may be lost in a disaster, measured in time; 24 hours promised, 5 minutes in practice (A7, 11.4)
RTO (recovery time objective)
how long service may be down while it is restored; 4 hours, proven by drill (A7)
runway
the days until a store is full at the current growth (11.3)
S3 (object storage)
the store for immutable files named by key; here originals, Parquet, exports and index files (6.6)
SameSite
a cookie flag that limits when a browser sends the cookie on requests from other sites (TH12)
SBOM
a software bill of materials: the list of every component in a build, kept beside the signed image (SR8)
schema-diff test
a CI test comparing the new API or format against the previous version's fixtures (6.7, 9)
scope
the set of data a principal may reach; always the session's organization and never a request value (SI1)
SDK
the vendor's client library that signs calls and parses replies; "the SDK" validates the cloud's responses in the entry-point table (10.2)
seam (reduction)
a way the demo is smaller than the platform, and the interface that stays so the full version can replace it (11.1)
Sec-Fetch-Site
a header the browser sets saying whether a request came from the same origin; state changes without it or a matching Origin are refused (9)
Secrets Manager
the store the provider key lives in, read by the owning task role only (10.6)
security group
a cloud firewall rule set that admits only the listed caller (10.5)
semantic diff
a comparison that shows what changed in meaning (a measure, a filter, a transition), not which characters moved (R5, 6.1)
separation of duties
no single role or person can both do a thing and approve it; the author never approves her own draft (10.5)
SERIALIZABLE
the isolation level under which transactions behave as if run one after another; PostgreSQL aborts one that would not (6.2)
Service token
the 5-minute token a role signs with its hourly KMS-certified key on every call to another role, naming caller, callee, organization, principal and epoch (SR3, 10.5). from the record's glossary
SHA-256 (ECDSA P-256, AES-256-GCM)
the hash, the signature curve and the authenticated cipher the record names for digests, service tokens and envelopes (10.6)
SHA-pinned (commit SHA)
a CI action referenced by its exact commit rather than a tag that can move (TH6)
SigV4
the cloud's request signing: every call to object storage or the key service is signed with the task role's credentials and carries the organization's encryption context, so the store and the key policy both check it (10.2)
silo
a separate database and key per organization; the rejected alternative to the pool (12.2)
SKIP LOCKED
a row-lock option that passes over rows another transaction holds, so many workers claim different jobs (6.4)
SLI (indicator)
the measured quantity an objective sets a target for, such as the p99 of the six-view refresh; shed requests are kept out of the latency ones (11.2, 11.3)
SLO (service level objective)
a target for a measured indicator over a window, with the budget it allows (11.3)
slug header
a request header naming an organization by its short name, which fAuth accepts as a fallback for finding a tenant; the platform ignores it and takes the organization from the signed token only (TH1)
snapshot (record snapshot, commit sequence)
the point in PostgreSQL's history a query's records were read at, named by a counter the receipt stores (6.3)
soft-delete (hold)
deletion that can be undone for a period; an organization's deletion waits 24 hours and can be cancelled (8, TH28)
Space
a company-defined area of apps inside an organization; Northstar's Security and Finance spaces (C01). from the record's glossary
Spike
the measurement that precedes a scene or release: the composition fixture on Forma 3.0.0 (review 4.3) and the demo's path from definition to reopen (A14). from the record's glossary
split brain
two nodes both believing they are the primary; ruled out by one writer by name (11.4)
SSE-KMS
object storage encrypting each object with a key held in the key management service; here one key per organization (10.6)
stale edit
an edit whose expected version is behind the record's current one; it conflicts into a recovery view, never a silent overwrite (7.3)
Static stability
each role's second task carrying the design point alone, so a zone loss needs no scaling action (11.1). from the record's glossary
stimulus
in the six-part quality scenario (source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response, measure), the event the system must respond to (4.2)
STRIDE
six threat categories: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege (10.4)
synchronous standby (Multi-AZ)
a second database copy that must have the bytes before a commit is acknowledged (6.6)
system interface
the host functions a WebAssembly module may call; here an input and an output stream only (SR5)
tags
the identifiers fields carry on the wire in the API and the shared formats; a removed field's tag is never given to a new field, so an old reader cannot misread it (9)
task role
the cloud identity an ECS task runs as; one per platform role, with its own grants (10.5)
threat actor
who attacks, with their capability and motive (10.3)
tombstone
a small marker left where data was deleted, carrying id, digests, actor and time but no payload (8)
TOTP
a one-time code from an authenticator app; the operators' second factor today (10.5)
trust boundaries (trust boundary)
a line on the data-flow diagram across which trust changes, drawn dashed and lettered B; each crossing gets a threat row (7)
trusted computing base
the components that enforce the invariants; everything else may fail without breaking them (10.2)
TTL
how long a DNS answer may be cached; it bounds how fast a failover takes effect (11.4)
Typed props
the server-computed, bounded values (flags, nested lists, SVG built from numbers) the renderer library accepts; no markup, no code (D1, 6.1). from the record's glossary
typed query
a query expressed in the grammar's operations rather than as SQL (D4)
versioning
object storage keeping previous versions of an object, so an overwrite or delete can be undone (8)
VPC
the private network the roles run in; boundary B2 (7)
WAF (web ACL)
the rule set in front of the load balancer that blocks hostile traffic patterns (6.6)
WCAG
the W3C's accessibility guidelines; level AA is the common conformance target (N12)
WebAssembly (WebAssembly sandbox)
a portable binary format run by a host that controls exactly which capabilities the code gets (SR5)
weighted target group
a load-balancer rule sending a chosen share of requests to the new build (11.1)
whole-output validation
the proposal is checked complete against the grammar and stored only if all of it passes; nothing partial (D8)
Workspace server
the one authorization point; serves pages and the JSON API, forwards typed queries and commands with the principal and epoch, and alone talks to fAuth and members (6.1). from the record's glossary
write skew
two transactions each reading a consistent premise and both committing changes that together break it; what SERIALIZABLE prevents (6.2)

Exercises

25 questions, each placed at the end of the section it follows. Answer in writing before opening the answer.

Exercise 1 after 1

The summary says D15's region door closes per organization. Before reading 5.3, predict what an organization that wants to move to another region a year in would have to move, and what it could leave behind. Then, when you reach 10.7, find the accepted risk that says why its backups do not shorten the list.

Answer

Everything made of the four one-way doors: its originals and Parquet revisions under its key, its PostgreSQL rows (records, work, publications, audit), the key itself, and the receipts that pin all of them; derived data (index files, caches, previews) can be left and rebuilt. Its backups stay in the region (AR10 in 10.7), so they are part of what moves, not a shortcut (1, 5.3, 8, 10.7).

Exercise 2 after 2

Suppose Maya's sheet had shown 228,000 with the label "bytes per minute over the observed events". The number is now honestly labelled. Argue which of section 2's six failures that label removes and which remain, then say what the design does that a well-labelled sheet cannot.

Answer

It removes only the missing denominator in step 3, and only for a reader who notices the label. Steps 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 remain: no source revision, a match rule in Maya's head, rows leaving the company, a verdict without its window and inventory revision, and an overwritable cell. The design binds the denominator into the definition (a 10-minute window) and the receipt pins it with the revisions and the rule, so a later reader cannot get 228,000 from the same app (2, R6, G3).

Exercise 3 after 3.3

A3 budgets the normalized copy at twice the originals. Predict which direction A3's 43.95 GiB moves if the spike measures Parquet revisions smaller than their CSV originals, say why the record budgets high anyway, and name the two numbers in section 11 that would shrink with it.

Answer

Down: the 29.3 GiB of Parquet is two thirds of the total, so a Parquet copy at the original's size would bring the 90-day figure to about 29.3 GiB. The record budgets twice "until measured" because only measured numbers are facts and an over-estimate errs toward spare disk. The data tasks' 50 GiB disk in 11.2 and the S3 line (60 GiB) would shrink (A3, 8, 11.2).

Exercise 4 after 4.2

A15's peak factor of 3.3 assumes every seat active at once. Rebuild the design point at a peak of 2 times average instead, carry it into 5.2's in-flight number and N1's 10x row, and say which numbers do not move.

Answer

18 operations a second times 2 is 36 at peak; at 100 ms that is 3.6 in flight, well inside one node's 8 slots; at 10x, 360 a second is 36 in flight, five data tasks plus one for a zone loss instead of eight plus one. The per-organization cap of 2, the p99.83 per operation, the contracts and every safety property do not move, which is exactly what A15's "if wrong" clause says (4.2, A15, 5.2, 11.2).

Exercise 5 after 5.2

Little's law gives 6 in flight at 100 ms. Suppose the spike measures a warm operation at 200 ms. Recompute, and say what breaks at the design point and what still holds.

Answer

60 a second times 0.2 s is 12 in flight, above the node's 8 slots, so the design point no longer fits one node and operations queue (429 past 20 waiting an organization). The per-organization cap of 2 makes a six-view refresh three waves of 200 ms, about 600 ms warm, still inside N3's 2 s, and nothing about isolation or receipts changes. Section 13.2's "a third task and a cap of 6" is the record's own prepared answer (5.2, 6.3, 13.2).

Exercise 6 after 5.3

D4 is a one-way door and DuckDB is not, though DuckDB is the engine that reads D4's Parquet. Explain the difference, using what a receipt pins.

Answer

A receipt pins revision digests, operator versions, parameters and a record snapshot, never an engine or a plan. Swapping DuckDB, or precomputing aggregates at admission, changes how a result is produced, and the re-derivation must still match; the Parquet layout and the PostgreSQL rows are what every receipt and every case is made of, so changing them migrates every organization (D4, 6.3, 12.2's D4 record).

Exercise 7 after 6.1

A colleague proposes caching the membership row for 30 s in the workspace server to save the 60 reads a second at peak. Name the requirement row the change breaks and the property the record pays for instead, and say what the proof of that property becomes with the cache.

Answer

N3's revocation row: an open display denied within 5 s, and "revocation proved by a read". With a 30 s cache a removed member keeps reading for up to 30 s and the proof becomes a staleness bound you argue about instead of a read you can test. The record spends two primary reads a request, 120 a second at peak, to keep it a read; section 10.2 later names the property as the fourth invariant (6.1, N3, 8).

Exercise 8 after 6.2

Make the case, in two sentences, for letting the workspace server write the publication under the author's session (alternative L), then say what the record protects by refusing it.

Answer

For: one fewer role to run, and one fewer hop on the publish path for a founder who runs everything alone. Against: the workspace server is the role that handles the member's request and forwards model output, so a flaw there could insert a publication nobody approved; D2 keeps the only publication writer one database grant away from model output, and SR3's test proves workspace cannot insert one (6.2, D2, 12.2).

Exercise 9 after 6.3

Swap the first two steps of the record command: check the expected version before looking up the idempotency outcome. Trace the lost-response retry of ik-1 and say what the member sees.

Answer

The first attempt committed version 1. The retry carries expected version 0; a version check first finds version 1 and returns 409 with a recovery view, so the member believes the decision failed and may submit it again under a new key, producing a second mutation or a confusing conflict. Outcome first finds ik-1 and returns the original outcome, one mutation (6.3, 7.3 messages 9 to 14, 9).

Exercise 10 after 6.4

Predict what a successful exploit of the XLSX parser can reach in this design, then what it could reach if the parser ran as ordinary code inside the worker process.

Answer

In the sandbox: one job's bytes and two streams; no socket, file or credentials endpoint, so the job fails visibly and nothing else is touched. In the worker process: the provider key, the ability to upload under any organization's key, and every revision the worker reads; 10.4 rates that row High on both scales before the sandbox (6.4, SR5).

Exercise 11 after 7.1

The provider returns a proposal with seven views that all parse and an eighth whose kind, "heatmap", no renderer is registered for. Predict what is stored, what Maya sees and what the slot does. Then change it: the eighth view is valid but the proposal has 25 views.

Answer

Both are refused whole. Admission checks every kind against a registered renderer and names the first check that failed; an unknown kind fails and nothing falls back, so no partial seven-view app exists, the draft is not admitted and the generation slot frees. Twenty-five views fails the complexity limit (at most 24) the same way. Maya sees the refusal with its reason, and R4 says the composer names the missing capability rather than inventing one (7.1 step 4, 6.2, R4, A5).

Exercise 12 after 7.2

Jordan downloads an export at 10:05; at 10:06 the administrator removes his grant while his canvas is open and one of his queries is still queued. Predict what the platform does about each of the three, and name the sentence in R11 that keeps the first honest.

Answer

The export is gone: delivered data is stated as unrecallable, and the record says so rather than pretending to a remote wipe. The canvas is denied within 5 s, because it polls the epoch every 5 s and every request reauthorizes. The queued query is re-checked at execution and again before release and returns denied, nothing cached or shown; R11's "revocation stops future results, queued ones included" is the rule, and "delivered data is stated as unrecallable" is the honest half (7.2, R11, 6.5).

Exercise 13 after 7.3

Two practitioners submit needs_context on EXP-002 at the same instant, both with expected version 0, with keys ik-1 and ik-9. Walk the transaction for each in 6.3's lock order and say what each sees. Then say what changes if both had sent the key ik-1.

Answer

Both insert their outcome rows (different keys, no clash); both take the record row FOR UPDATE; one wins, finds the record absent, commits version 1. The other waits on the row lock, then finds version 1 where it expected 0 and returns 409 with the recovery view: one commit, one visible conflict, never last-writer-wins. With the same key, nothing changes between two principals, because the key is scoped to the principal; for one principal retrying, the second insert waits on the outcome row and returns the stored outcome, one mutation (7.3, 6.3, 9).

Exercise 14 after 8

A result cache keyed by (view, parameters) alone would be fast and simple. Name the two guarantees from section 4 it breaks, give one concrete wrong answer it would serve, and say what the record keys the cache by instead.

Answer

N7 (nothing of one organization reaches another): the canary with the same view and parameters would receive Northstar's total. And N3's and N5's revocation bound: a result computed for Jordan before his grant was removed would be served after it. The key is the receipt digest, which carries the organization, revisions, record sequence, parameters and policy epoch, and a hit is still re-authorized before release; 10.2 later names the two properties as its first and fourth invariants (8, 6.3, N7, N5).

Exercise 15 after 9

Argue for returning 403 rather than 404 to a member of another organization who opens Northstar's work id (it is more honest, and clients can show a better message). Then say what property of the error model it would give up, and why the one 403 the record does return is safe.

Answer

A 403 tells the caller the id exists and belongs to someone, which is a one-bit leak per guess and, across many guesses, a map of another organization's work; the record's rule is that denied, foreign and absent are indistinguishable. The author's own-approval 403 is safe because she already sees the app, so no existence is revealed, and naming the rule tells her what to do (9, R11, 7.3's canary case).

Exercise 16 after 10.2

The island drops any page whose epoch is behind, and polls the membership epoch every 5 s, yet it is excluded from the trusted computing base. Argue why that is correct.

Answer

The island runs on the member's machine, where TA3 already holds everything it holds, so nothing it enforces can be relied on. The server re-checks membership at execution and before release, and a query carries its epoch so the server, not the island, can refuse a stale one; the island's discard improves what the member sees, it does not decide what they may see (10.2, SI4, 7.2).

Exercise 17 after 10.4

Rewrite TH5 for a design where an approval is "approve draft 7" with no digest. Which prevent control vanishes, what sequence does the attacker run, and which of the remaining controls still holds?

Answer

M10's digest binding vanishes. Maya asks Sarah to approve draft 7, Sarah approves, Maya patches the denominator into revision 8, and the publisher publishes "draft 7's current content", which Sarah never saw. The CHECK that approver is not author still holds, and so does the epoch check, but neither is about content; G2's "a stale approval is refused" becomes impossible to test (TH5, 6.2, G2).

Exercise 18 after 10.5

A service token minted by the workspace server for Maya at epoch 7, callee the data service, is captured inside the VPC at 10:00:00. List what an attacker can do with it and until when, then what they cannot do and which fact stops each attempt.

Answer

They can call the data service as Maya, within her organization and her permissions, until 10:05:00, which is what AR3 accepts. They cannot call the control plane (the token names its callee), publish or change policy (the data service holds no such grant), act after an administrator revokes Maya (the callee re-reads the membership row), or act after 10:05 (expiry); and a replaced task rotates the signing keys (10.5, SR3, AR3, 10.6).

Exercise 19 after 10.7

AR2 accepts that a compromised data service can read every organization's revisions. Design the control that would remove AR2, cost it against A8 and N10, and say whether the per-organization keys already limit the exposure.

Answer

The control is a data task (or a whole cell, or a silo) per organization, so one credential unwraps one key. The cost is what D3's record names: ten stacks now and a hundred at N1 for one operator, and a second data task per organization in a cost table already dominated by the data service. The keys do not limit it, because the data service's role legitimately unwraps every organization's key with its context; what bounds AR2 is detection, the canary suite each release, and the escape hatch, moving one organization to a cell when it matters (AR2, D3, 11.2, 12.2).

Exercise 20 after 11.1

Wave one of a release doubles the six-view refresh's p99 from 400 ms to 900 ms, with no errors and no receipt mismatches. Using only 11.1, say whether the wave rolls back and what else in 11.1 can stop a release, then explain why the rollback metric was made that narrow.

Answer

No: forma_canary_failures_total alone rolls a wave back, and it counts errors, cross-tenant hits and receipt mismatches, not latency. 11.1's other brake is "any page of 11.3 blocks the next wave", and 900 ms is inside N3's 2 s, so no page fires; the regression is caught over the month by the refresh objective's budget. The metric is isolation and correctness because those are the failures a rollback must never wait on a human for; latency has budgets and pages (11.1, N3, 11.3).

Exercise 21 after 11.2

Rebuild the Fargate line from the sizes and unit prices, with disk at $0.000111 per GiB-hour and only the data tasks carrying the 50 GiB of disk the record sizes, then the data service's share, then the number of data tasks at 10x.

Answer

13 vCPU × 730 h × $0.04048 is about $384 and 54 GiB × 730 × $0.004445 about $175, together $559; two data tasks × 50 GiB × 730 × $0.000111 add about $8, so about $565. The data service's two tasks are 8 vCPU and 32 GiB, about $236 plus $104, the "$340" the record names, plus their disk. At 10x, 600 a second × 0.1 s is 60 in flight, at 8 a node eight tasks, plus one for a zone loss (11.2, 5.2).

Exercise 22 after 11.3

AL6, the oldest queued job over 10 minutes, is a ticket; AL11, an audit or anchor write failure, is a page. Argue the split from the properties each protects.

Answer

A late job is a liveness delay on a cold path the member already sees as queued within 1 s; nothing is wrong about what they see, so it can wait for morning. A failed audit write means actions are happening without the append-only record SI5 promises, a safety property, and the longer it runs the larger the gap; that is worth waking someone (11.3, SI5, N3).

Exercise 23 after 12.2

Option B under D1, both representations at once, is dismissed in one sentence. Make its best case for the demo, then show which of G2's done-when clauses it strains and why the deferred custom-widget tier is not the same thing as B.

Answer

For B: the generation moment could show a bespoke widget where the typed vocabulary shows assembly (RK6), and an app could use the best fit per view. G2 requires a publication to bind exact definition and renderer identities and a reviewer to approve exactly what runs; with two representations the reviewer approves two kinds of artifact through two admission paths, one of them needing a sanitizer, which is what "doubles what a reviewer approves" means, and N7 pays for the second path. The custom-widget tier is the markup path deferred behind its own tickets and its own threat model, not a second path in this release's approval flow (12.2, D1, G2, 3.2).

Exercise 24 after 13.1

RK5, the unmeasured cold aggregate, is Medium. Argue for High, then say why the record's rank holds.

Answer

For High: the six-view refresh at 2 s is N3's critical row and a miss touches every published app. The rank holds because the fallback, aggregates computed at admission, changes DuckDB's plan and not the grammar, the receipts or D4, so no one-way door and no isolation property is at stake, which is 13.1's definition of High (13.1, 12.2's D4 record, 5.2).

Exercise 25 after C

The two 99.9% factors for the platform's own roles are the record's assumption, not a vendor figure. Argue whether two tasks in two zones justify it and what measurement would replace it; then compose the warm and cold chains from appendix C's hard rows and say why one full restore does not fit N2's month.

Answer

Two tasks in two zones means a zone loss or one task's crash leaves a task sized to carry the design point, so the figure assumes the remaining failures are deploys and bugs; only the failure-mode drills and a quarter of real-user availability data can replace it. Warm: 0.999 (CloudFront) × 0.9995 (RDS) × 0.999 (workspace) × 0.999 (data) is about 0.9965; cold adds S3 at 0.999 and KMS at 0.99999, about 0.9955. 99.5% of 730 hours allows 3.65 hours, 219 minutes; a 4-hour restore is 240, 21 minutes over, so N2 assumes no full restore in a month (C, 5.2, N2, 11.4).

Flashcards

Click a card to flip it. "Got it" retires a card until you reset the deck; "Again" puts it back a few cards later. Progress is kept in this browser. The same cards are in flashcards.tsv for Anki (File, Import, fields front, back, deck).

Reading

The topics this design touches first, then the rest. Primary sources where they exist: the standard, the vendor's own documentation, the free chapters.

For this design

Writing and reading design documents

  • Design Docs at Google (Malte Ubl) what a design document is for, the sections most carry and why, and the case for writing down the alternatives.
  • Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals the public index of a large project's design proposals, by area, stage and release; the KEP template in the kubernetes/enhancements repository carries the production-readiness questionnaire.
  • Rust RFC book a language's accepted design proposals, one page each; new ones start from the template linked below.
  • Rust RFC template a "guide-level" explanation that teaches the change, then a "reference-level" one that specifies it.
  • Fuchsia RFC best practices include a detail only if it has material impact, asked there as whether anyone would change their vote because of it.
  • Google technical writing courses courses for engineers who write; Technical Writing One, on its own page, teaches clear, short sentences, lists and focused paragraphs.

Decisions and trade-offs

  • Documenting architecture decisions (Michael Nygard) the decision record in five parts: title, context, decision, status, consequences; adr.github.io credits it with popularising the form.
  • Markdown Architectural Decision Records (MADR) a decision-record template with the considered options, the outcome, the consequences and a confirmation, the form the alternatives section follows.
  • Amazon's 2015 shareholder letter the one-way door and two-way door distinction, in its original words.
  • Fundamentals of Software Architecture the book's companion site, with its architecture katas; the book's first chapter (not on the site) states the first law, that everything in software architecture is a trade-off, which the decision records practise.

Multi-tenant systems

  • Tenancy models for a multitenant solution (Microsoft) tenancy models, isolation, noisy neighbours and the cost of each choice.
  • Silo, pool and bridge models (AWS SaaS Lens) dedicating or sharing resources per tenant, and the bridge between them, where some layers are siloed and others pooled.
  • Google Identity Platform multi-tenancy identity tenants, each with its own users and sign-in providers, inside one project.

Data stores, isolation and pagination

  • Row security policies (PostgreSQL) policies the database applies to every row a role reads or writes, once row security is enabled on the table; table owners are exempt unless the table forces them, and superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS always are.
  • Transaction isolation (PostgreSQL) what read committed, repeatable read and serializable promise.
  • Use The Index, Luke: fetching the next page why offsets get slower with every page, and the seek method, keyset pagination, that does not.
  • Partitioned tables (BigQuery) how a time partition bounds what a query scans.
  • Clustered tables (BigQuery) sorting within a partition so filters on a few columns read less.
  • BI Engine (BigQuery) BigQuery's in-memory analysis service: what it caches, and how a reservation sizes it.
  • Transactional outbox writing an event in the same transaction as the row, so it is never lost; the relay may send it twice, so consumers must be idempotent.
  • Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe) the idempotency key, and what to do when the same request arrives twice.
  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications the book's site; the book is the source of the consistency, partitioning and fault-model vocabulary used here.

Threat modeling and secure design

  • Threat modeling cheat sheet (OWASP) the four questions, the process and the output a threat model should have.
  • STRIDE threats (Microsoft) the six categories, each defined, most with an example.
  • Threat Modeling Manifesto the values and the anti-patterns, in one page.
  • Building Secure and Reliable Systems (Google) readable online; invariants, least privilege and recovery, and in chapter 6 the trusted computing base.
  • Application Security Verification Standard (OWASP) the verification standard: requirement lists, downloadable as CSV and JSON, for designing, building and testing web applications.
  • Secure design principles (NCSC) establish the context, make compromise difficult, make disruption difficult, make compromise detection easier, and reduce its impact.

Authentication, sessions and OAuth

  • OpenID Connect Core the ID token, its claims and how a relying party validates it.
  • OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) the authorization code flow, refresh tokens and scopes.
  • OAuth 2.0 threat model (RFC 6819) what goes wrong with tokens, and the countermeasures.
  • OAuth 2.0 security best current practice (RFC 9700) the current security advice, which updates RFC 6749 and RFC 6819.
  • Session management cheat sheet (OWASP) cookie flags, lifetimes, rotation and revocation.
  • CSRF prevention cheat sheet (OWASP) why a cookie alone is not enough for a mutation.
  • Identity-Aware Proxy overview a central authorization layer for applications reached over HTTPS, checking identity before the request reaches the app.
  • Service account impersonation (Google Cloud IAM) how one principal acts as a service account through short-lived credentials instead of a key.

Queues, jobs and background work

  • Cloud Run request timeout one platform's ceiling on a request's life, up to an hour, and its advice to make long requests idempotent and resumable.
  • Pub/Sub push subscriptions push delivery to an HTTPS endpoint, its acknowledgement deadline, redelivery and authenticated push.
  • Understand Cloud Tasks scheduled and rate-limited delivery of work to a service.
  • Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Amazon Builders' Library) the age of messages in the queue as the backlog signal, and fairness between tenants.
  • Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library) the retry rules behind every "with backoff" in the failure table.

Operating, deploying and observing

  • Monitoring distributed systems (SRE book) the four golden signals and what to page on.
  • Automating safe, hands-off deployments (Amazon Builders' Library) waves, bake time and automatic rollback.
  • Using load shedding to avoid overload (Amazon Builders' Library) goodput, and what to drop first.
  • Postmortem culture (SRE book) blameless postmortems, and the follow-up actions that keep an incident from recurring.
  • Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework recommendations by pillar for systems on Google Cloud.
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework the same idea by pillar for systems on AWS.

Requirements, numbers and service levels

  • Latency numbers every programmer should know the ladder of costs, from an L1 cache reference past a round trip across an ocean, now with rows for model calls, that estimates start from.
  • Service Level Objectives (Google SRE book) why percentiles, what an objective is for, and why 100 percent is the wrong target.
  • Implementing SLOs (SRE workbook) a step-by-step recipe for choosing indicators and setting objectives, and a pointer to the workbook's example SLO document.
  • arc42 quality requirements the scenario form, with a source, a stimulus and a measurable response.

Builds, packages and the release path

  • SLSA build track (v1.2) the build levels, each a stronger guarantee about how an artefact was built and how hard its provenance is to forge.
  • Secure use reference (GitHub Actions) one CI platform's hardening: script injection, locking or pinning third-party actions, OpenID Connect instead of stored cloud keys.
  • Generating provenance statements (npm) one registry's signed link from a package to the source and the build that produced it, and how consumers verify it.

Front ends in the browser

  • TanStack Table the headless grid that leaves the markup to the design system.
  • TanStack Query server state in the browser: caching, and refetching in the background.
  • Progress indicators (Nielsen Norman Group) a looped spinner for waits of 2 to 10 seconds, a percent-done bar for longer ones, and why the bar makes a long wait tolerable.
  • Render and Commit (React) trigger, render, commit: the steps from a change of state to the screen, in one framework's words.
  • Intro to reactivity (Solid) signals and their subscribers, so that a change updates only what reads it.
  • Islands architecture (Astro) interactive components on an otherwise static, server-rendered page, each hydrated on its own.
  • Web Vitals (web.dev) loading, interactivity and visual stability, measured on real page loads and assessed at the 75th percentile.
  • Strict Content Security Policy (web.dev) a nonce- or hash-based policy with 'strict-dynamic' against cross-site scripting, and its limits.
  • require-trusted-types-for (MDN) the directive that controls what may reach the DOM's script-injection sinks.

Diagrams that say something

  • The C4 model context, containers, components, code: the four hierarchical levels this document's pictures follow.
  • C4 diagram notation what every box and arrow must carry to be readable without its author.
  • C4 review checklist the questions to ask of any architecture diagram before it ships.
  • Mermaid sequence diagrams the syntax behind the sequence diagram in the data flows section.
  • System modeling (OWASP threat modeling cheat sheet) data-flow diagrams that show trust boundaries, flows, stores and processes, the form section 7 uses so that section 10 can cite it.
